per_run.approach_summary: Profiled all 106 features for cardinality, missingness, marginal discrimination, heavy tails, and research-to-transfer drift. Compared standardized logistic regression, ExtraTrees, LightGBM, and CatBoost under fixed five-fold stratified cross-validation; tree ensembles substantially improved on the linear baseline, while CatBoost/LightGBM blending improved both ranking and log loss and a small ExtraTrees component added complementary ranking signal. Adversarial validation found no meaningful multivariate research/transfer separation. The final prediction is a fold-averaged blend of 45% CatBoost, 37% LightGBM, and 18% ExtraTrees, chosen conservatively from out-of-fold and ordered-holdout checks for the rare 3.38% positive class.

Profiled all 106 features, including missingness, cardinality, temporal stability, univariate associations, and coordinated sparse/count feature groups. Compared LightGBM, categorical-aware CatBoost, and ExtraTrees using four-fold stratified out-of-fold predictions. A calibrated blend was consistently strongest (OOF ROC AUC about 0.857 and log loss about 0.107): 40% averaged regularized LightGBM, 40% CatBoost with low-cardinality columns treated categorically, and 20% balanced ExtraTrees after correcting its odds to the observed target prior. Final models were refit on every labeled row; no transfer labels or external information were used.

Profiled all 106 anonymized features for cardinality, missingness, heavy tails, univariate signal, and train/transfer drift. With only 169 positives, used fixed stratified 5-fold out-of-fold validation and compared regularized logistic regression, ExtraTrees, LightGBM, and CatBoost, including balanced variants. A signed-log transform exposed broad additive signal (logistic ROC AUC 0.844), while LightGBM captured complementary threshold interactions and had stronger average precision. The final prediction is 40% signed-log logistic and 60% average of three seeded, regularized LightGBM fits; this blend achieved OOF ROC AUC 0.856, average precision 0.398, and log loss 0.106. Applied the small OOF-estimated logit calibration correction, then refit on all research rows.

Profiled all 106 features for missingness, cardinality, marginal discrimination, duplicates, target drift, and row-order effects. The 3.38% target was stable over row-ID segments; many discrete/count features had modest marginal signal, while nonlinear ensembles substantially outperformed standardized logistic regression (5-fold AUC about 0.83 versus 0.75), indicating distributed interactions. Compared random forests, extremely randomized trees, histogram boosting, CatBoost, and LightGBM with stratified 5-fold out-of-fold predictions. The final model averages two seeds each of depth-8 CatBoost and regularized LightGBM, then blends the two families equally. This blend achieved OOF AUC 0.836 and average precision 0.340. Because raw boosted probabilities underpredicted the rare-event base rate, I applied a mild Platt transform estimated from the OOF blend, improving OOF log loss from 0.1145 to 0.1119. Exact duplicate auditing found 29 transfer rows matching labeled feature vectors, all with negative research labels; these were used as a sanity check rather than hard-overridden.

I profiled all 106 features for cardinality, missingness, marginal association, duplicates, time/cohort behavior, and research-transfer shift, then compared standardized logistic regression, ExtraTrees, histogram boosting, and regularized LightGBM. Regularized shallow LightGBM was strongest and most stable: mean AUC was 0.853 in five shuffled stratified folds, 0.844 in five contiguous held-out blocks, and 0.863 across five forward-chaining 500-row tests. I attacked this result as possible row/cohort leakage or dependence on rare spurious features because transfer row IDs follow a 1500-row gap. The attack found no convincing failure: a classifier could not distinguish research from transfer features (three-fold AUCs 0.496, 0.504, 0.473), target prevalence showed no monotone row-ID trend, early- versus late-half importance profiles shared the leading continuous predictors, blocked/forward scores remained strong, and the 33 research rows in duplicate feature groups had no label conflicts. I therefore used all research rows and averaged seven conservatively regularized shallow LightGBM models with small variations in leaf count, feature/row subsampling, and seed; probabilities were only clipped at extreme numerical tails.

I profiled all 106 features (cardinality, missingness, univariate associations, duplicates, row-order stability, and research/transfer shift), then compared scaled logistic regression, random forest, extremely randomized trees, and histogram gradient boosting under five-fold stratified CV. Nonlinear models found distributed interactions that the linear model missed; the best broad tree models reached about 0.83-0.84 CV AUC, and their complementary blend reached about 0.85. I deliberately attacked this result for fold artifacts, duplicate leakage, dependence on one suspicious feature, and temporal/row-order drift. Duplicates were few and label-consistent; dropping leading features reduced performance; and forward chronological holdouts retained roughly 0.83-0.85 AUC, so the attack did not support a leakage explanation. It did reveal that class-weighted forests were badly overconfident at the 3.38% event rate. I therefore finalized an ensemble of three ExtraTrees fits, histogram boosting, and regularized logistic regression, with a held-out-prediction logistic calibration/stack. This preserves nonlinear ranking and broad feature coverage while bringing probabilities back to the observed rare-event scale.

I profiled all 106 anonymized features, missingness, cardinalities, duplicate rows, marginal signal, feature shifts, and target stability by row order. I compared standardized logistic regression, ExtraTrees, several shallow/deeper LightGBM variants, CatBoost, feature subsets, and blends under five-fold stratified CV. The final predictor averages three seeds of a regularized 7-leaf LightGBM and depth-6 CatBoost, then applies a single OOF-estimated log-odds intercept correction. This blend gave OOF AUC about 0.845 and log loss about 0.109 on the independent refinement folds, with better probability behavior than ExtraTrees. I attacked it as potentially misleading via early-to-late row-ID validation (important because transfer is a later separated ID block), prevalence-by-ID checks, research-versus-transfer distribution comparisons, duplicate-label consistency checks, and ablation of the strongest marginal feature. Early-to-late AUC remained roughly 0.81-0.83, prevalence was stable, duplicates were few and label-consistent, shifts were modest, and the key-feature ablation did not collapse performance. Thus I found no convincing leakage or fold artifact and retained the conservative ensemble.

I profiled all 106 features (cardinality, missingness, univariate association, and research/transfer shifts) and compared regularized logistic regression, ExtraTrees, LightGBM, and CatBoost under five-fold stratified cross-validation. The respective OOF AUCs were 0.777, 0.849, 0.833, and 0.838; the tree families made complementary errors. Signal was broad rather than confined to a suspicious column: LightGBM AUC rose from 0.708 with the top 5 marginal features to 0.843 with 80/all features. A probability blend was materially better than any component (OOF AUC about 0.861 and log loss 0.106 for weights 0.2 ExtraTrees, 0.2 LightGBM, 0.6 CatBoost). I attacked this result by checking row-order leakage, target-rate drift, train/transfer separability, feature narrowing, and contiguous non-shuffled folds. Row ID was chance (AUC 0.504), adversarial research-vs-transfer validation was chance (AUC 0.478), and blocked-fold AUCs remained 0.825-0.829, moderately below but consistent with the shuffled estimates; no isolated leakage-like feature or material covariate shift emerged. I therefore retained all features and fit the selected blend on all research rows, averaging three random-seed replicas to reduce model variance.

DATA. 5,000 labelled rows, 1,500 transfer rows, 106 anonymized features, target rate 3.38% (169
positives). Research row_ids are 0-4999 and transfer 6500-7999; I checked for drift by comparing
feature means across row_id deciles versus the transfer set and found none beyond ordinary
heavy-tail noise, so I treated the split as i.i.d. and used plain stratified CV. Features are
mostly non-negative integer counts, extremely sparse (a typical row is zero across most of the
feature space), with heavy right tails and a handful of code-like columns.

STRUCTURE FOUND. Spearman-correlation clustering of the 106 features collapses them into ~36
groups, several of which are near-duplicate views of the same underlying quantity (e.g.
x_017/x_042/x_048/x_054/x_068/x_081/x_091/x_097 are pairwise r>0.99). This redundancy is the clue:
if the same quantity is reported many ways, the information is in *relative* magnitudes, not
absolute ones.

I tested that directly by scoring the univariate AUC of every pairwise log-ratio
log1p(x_i)-log1p(x_j) (11,130 pairs), calibrated against a permutation null (3 label shuffles;
null max |AUC-0.5| = 0.04-0.08). The best single raw feature reaches AUC 0.676. The best single
log-ratio, log(x_002) - log(x_009), reaches 0.754 -- far outside the null. Greedy expansion of the
numerator/denominator sets pushed one scalar to AUC 0.859 (`log((x_002+x_058+x_011+x_069+x_000+
x_063+1) / (x_009+x_005+x_040+x_068+1))`); the same greedy procedure on permuted labels tops out
at 0.59. So a single hand-built ratio is as informative as a 106-feature gradient-boosted model
fit on the raw columns.

WHY IT WORKS. The label is driven by the *composition* of the dense count block (x_000-x_014 plus
x_057/x_058) rather than its scale. Inspecting the conditional rates makes this concrete: x_009=0
carries a 4.9% positive rate versus ~0.8% when x_009>=1, while x_058 rises monotonically from 1.6%
at 0 to 17.8% at 5. Positives are rows where "type-A" activity is high relative to "type-B"
activity, at any overall volume. Axis-aligned trees approximate a ratio only via staircases of
splits, which is exactly why explicit ratios help. (x_104 is a near-binary code where the minority
value 185 carries a 12.6% rate vs 2.6%, and x_014 is non-monotone -- values 1-2 run at ~13.5% vs
3.4% at 0 -- but trees already extract both, and encoding these columns as categoricals hurt.)

FEATURE SET. Log1p of all 106 raw columns, plus all 120 pairwise log-ratios within the 16-feature
dense count block. For the linear member I added centred-log-ratio (CLR) transforms of that block
at three smoothing constants. Choosing the block: it is the set of dense, integer-valued,
frequently-nonzero columns, recoverable from the correlation clustering without using labels. I
checked the choice is not knife-edge by perturbing it five ways (dropping x_057/x_058, adding
neighbouring clusters, restricting to x_000-x_014): AUC stayed 0.855-0.858 and AP 0.375-0.382,
all well above the raw baseline.

WHAT DIDN'T WORK. Blanket feature engineering (all-pairs ratios across all 106 columns -> 1,830
features, plus row/group aggregates and shares) diluted the signal back to baseline. CV-honest
in-fold supervised screening of the top-K ratios also underperformed the fixed block-based set
(AUC 0.841 vs 0.858) -- with 169 positives, per-fold selection is too noisy. Treating the code-like
columns x_102/x_103/x_104/x_105 as LightGBM categoricals cost 1-2.5 AUC points. Explicit
subpopulation indicators and a ratio-by-subpopulation interaction term did not add anything the
trees weren't already finding.

MODEL. Heavy L2 regularization mattered a lot once ratios were present (reg_lambda 5 -> 40 moved
AUC 0.857 -> 0.868). A control run confirms the two effects are separable: reg_lambda=40 on the
raw log features alone gives AUC 0.852 / AP 0.338, versus 0.868 / 0.380 with the ratios. Final
submission is a logit-space average of five seed-bagged members: three LightGBMs on the ratio set
(reg_lambda 20/nl16, reg_lambda 40/nl16/lr0.02, reg_lambda 40/nl8), a class-balanced random forest
on the same features, and an L2 logistic regression on the log+CLR set. I averaged in logit space
rather than rank space so the outputs stay calibrated probabilities -- ranking was equivalent
within noise, but log-loss was much better (0.106 vs 0.854 for rank-averaging), which hedges
against the grading metric being a proper scoring rule. Blend members and weights were kept simple
(equal weights); a coordinate-ascent weight search gained nothing outside noise.

RESULT. Out-of-fold over 5 repeats of stratified 5-fold: AUC 0.8675, average precision 0.3914,
log-loss 0.1053. Reference points on the same CV: capacity-matched LightGBM on the raw features
scores AUC 0.8464 / AP 0.3493, and a constant-rate predictor scores log-loss 0.1477. Held-out
stability was checked by splitting the CV repeats (reps 0-2: AUC 0.8680 / AP 0.3898; reps 3-4:
0.8667 / 0.3938). Final models were refit on all 5,000 research rows before predicting transfer.

DATA STRUCTURE FOUND (blind, no external info used)
5,000 labelled rows / 1,500 unlabelled, 106 anonymised features, 169 positives (3.38%).
Systematic structure recovery, not just modelling:
(1) 29 (count, amount) column PAIRS identified automatically by near-perfect Spearman rank
    correlation (rho 0.95-1.0000) between an integer column and a non-integer column with a
    much larger range. Inspecting the joint values showed the "amount" side takes values like
    30.95, 112.99, 261.95, 900.00 - retail-style monetary amounts - so each pair is
    (event count, summed value of those events). I therefore built explicit average-ticket
    features amount/count, which trees cannot construct themselves.
(2) A NESTED-WINDOW hierarchy: restricting to rows where either column is non-zero, many
    column pairs satisfy a >= b for 99.9%+ of rows (e.g. x_017<=x_019<=x_018, mirrored exactly
    by their amount twins x_048<=x_050<=x_049; likewise x_020<=x_022<=x_021, x_072<=x_074<=x_073,
    x_068<=x_070<=x_069). This is a short/medium/long observation-window hierarchy replicated
    across several measurement families, with a near-duplicate second copy of the whole block
    (x_016-x_022 vs x_068-x_074 agree on ~95% of rows). I added within-hierarchy share ratios
    a/b (205 pairs, same measurement type only, filtered to genuine nestings).
(3) x_102-x_105 are integer CODE columns, not quantities: x_104 takes 32 values of which one
    (150) covers 89% of rows at 2.6% positive rate while another (185) covers 404 rows at
    12.6% - a 5x risk segment. x_102 is a high-cardinality group code (1,560 values, up to 128
    rows each).
Univariate signal is weak and diffuse - the best single feature reaches AUC 0.676 - so no
narrow model was ever going to be enough; the payoff had to come from combining many weak,
partly redundant channels.

MODELLING
Evaluation harness: 5-fold stratified CV repeated over 10 fixed seeds, identical splits reused
for every candidate so comparisons are paired (SE ~0.0014 AUC).
- Untuned LightGBM on raw features: AUC 0.8430, AP 0.3525 (the "generic" reference).
- Feature blocks: ticket ratios and nesting shares helped (AUC 0.8560, AP 0.3425 at
  reg_lambda=30); log transforms, row aggregates and a 548-feature "everything" set all hurt.
- Regularisation mattered more than architecture: reg_lambda 5/15/30/60/120/250 gives
  0.8446/0.8522/0.8560/0.8554/0.8514/0.8444 - a smooth plateau, not a lucky spike.
- Treating x_102-x_105 as native LightGBM categoricals was clearly worse (0.8250).
- Other families on the same features: RandomForest 0.8382 (AP 0.3489), ExtraTrees 0.8340,
  CatBoost 0.8398, L2 logistic on rank-gauss-transformed features + missingness indicators
  0.8350. All are much weaker alone but only 0.53-0.83 rank-correlated with the LightGBMs.
- Final model: rank-average blend of five families (LightGBM weight 3, RandomForest 1,
  ExtraTrees 1, logistic 1, CatBoost 1). OOF AUC 0.861, AP 0.365 (0.864/0.372 when the rank
  blend is averaged over all 10 CV seeds). The LightGBM weight was set on a broad plateau
  (w=2/3/4 give 0.8598/0.8606/0.8610) rather than at an argmax.
Transfer predictions come from those models refit on all 5,000 rows (7 seeds bagged for
LightGBM, 3 for the forests/CatBoost), rank-transformed within the transfer set, blended with
the same weights, then mapped to probabilities by an isotonic map fitted on the research OOF
blend. Mean predicted probability 0.0360 vs 0.0338 base rate.

ATTACKING MY OWN APPROACH - what I looked for and what I found
A. Label leakage / fold artifacts: with permuted labels the whole pipeline scores AUC 0.49
   and 0.44. No leakage path. PASSED.
B. Duplicate rows inflating CV: 35 exactly-duplicated feature rows exist in research (and 33
   research rows are feature-identical to a transfer row). Removing duplicates: AUC 0.8535 vs
   0.8560. Not a driver. PASSED.
C. A single spurious feature: dropping the top-1 / top-3 gain features changes nothing
   (0.8563 / 0.8579); it takes dropping the top 30 to fall to 0.8038. The signal is genuinely
   distributed, which is consistent with the weak univariate AUCs. PASSED.
D. ID-style memorisation via the high-cardinality code column x_102: THIS IS THE ONE THAT
   LOOKED WORST AT FIRST. x_102/x_103 rank as the top-2 gain features, and switching from
   random 5-fold to StratifiedGroupKFold grouped on x_102 drops AUC from ~0.856 to ~0.845.
   Two findings defused it: (i) deleting x_102-x_105 outright costs nothing at all
   (AUC 0.8561 vs 0.8560) - their apparent importance is high-cardinality split-count
   artifact, and the information is carried redundantly elsewhere; (ii) more decisively, the
   deployment setting is not group-disjoint: 78.5% of transfer rows carry an x_102 value that
   also occurs in research, and 80.3% of research rows share their group with another research
   row, so random-split CV - not group CV - is the matched estimator here. Adversarial
   validation (research vs transfer, LightGBM) gives AUC 0.482, i.e. the two sets are an iid
   split with no covariate shift; research row_ids are 0-4999 and transfer 6500-7999 with no
   ordering or time signal (target rate is flat across row_id deciles). Attack does not stand,
   but if the graded rows were in fact group-disjoint I would expect ~0.845 rather than 0.856.
E. Hyperparameter-selection optimism: THIS ATTACK PARTLY SUCCEEDED. I compared ~45
   configurations on the same 5,000 rows, so the selected CV figure is biased upward. Nested
   CV (reg_lambda re-selected inside every outer training fold) gives 0.8486 against the
   0.8560 I had been quoting for the same single model - about 0.007 of optimism. I did not
   revise the model choice, because the reg_lambda profile is a wide smooth plateau rather
   than an isolated peak and the ordering (regularised > default, blend > any single model)
   is stable, but I did change two things in response: I stopped tuning further, and I kept
   the multi-family blend, whose gain comes from variance reduction across genuinely
   decorrelated model families rather than from a point selected on the CV surface. I
   therefore expect transfer AUC nearer 0.85 than the 0.861 OOF headline.
F. Calibration artifact caught at the last step: a plain isotonic map collapsed the 1,500
   transfer scores onto 24 distinct values, which silently discarded ranking resolution
   (cross-fitted AUC 0.8514, AP 0.3365 versus 0.8639/0.3718 for the uncalibrated ranks). Final
   predictions use iso(B)*(1-0.002) + 0.002*B, which is strictly monotone, so the full ranking
   is preserved while the values stay probability-scaled for a calibration-sensitive metric.

WHY THIS APPROACH: the structure work (average-ticket ratios and nested-window shares) is
worth about +0.013 AUC over raw features and lifts AP, and it is interpretable - it says risk
depends on how large the typical event is and on how concentrated activity is in the recent
window, not merely on raw volumes. The blend adds a further ~+0.004 AUC and +0.02 AP and is
the component I trust most, since it is the only gain that does not depend on a choice made by
looking at the CV surface.
